blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en: Answers from generative AI chatbots built on large language models (LLMs) now arrive at very different speeds: reasoning models deliberate before replying, while response caches can return a stored answer at once. Blind preference votes, which rank these models, are read as judgments of their text, and if delivery matters, faster answers are expected to gain. Research on the labor illusion and on how text appears on screen suggests instead that an answer which unfolds as it is written is credited over the same answer shown at once. We test these accounts with three sources of variation in natural use. First, compar:IA, a French government chatbot arena, answered repeated prompts, by a random draw, either with a fresh answer streamed as it was written or with a stored earlier answer from the same model, shown at once. Within the same prompt, a replay lowered an answer's chance of winning a decisive blind vote by 25.8 percentage points. The same stored text won 57% of its decisive votes when streamed and 29% when replayed, and voters called it less complete, more superficial and more often incorrect when replayed. Second, provider congestion slowed streamed answers. In 324,029 conversations, slower answers earned no detectable net credit in the vote, but a slower first exchange made visitors less likely to ask a follow-up question. Third, in 4,378,514 WildChat replies from everyday ChatGPT use, replies slowed by congestion made users less likely to continue. Delivery moved blind votes, in the direction opposite to the one the arena's designers expected, while waiting cost follow-up questions that a comparison between two answers cannot register when both are slow. The results bear on how AI services cache and stream answers, how they budget latency, and how preference leaderboards evaluate models.

blocks.en: 1 Introduction
blocks.zh: 导言

blocks.en:
How long an AI system takes to answer has become a design choice. Reasoning models are built to spend more
computation, and therefore more time, before they reply ( Guo et al., 2025 ; Snell et al., 2025 ) .
At the same time, engineers work to make answers arrive faster: speculative decoding shortens generation ( Leviathan et al., 2023 ) , and response caches return a stored answer to a repeated question almost at once ( Bang, 2023 ) . Chatbot providers now offer “fast” and “thinking” modes side by side. Whether users
see an answer appear instantly, watch it being written, or wait while the system thinks is decided every day by
product teams, usually on cost grounds.

blocks.en:
Blind preference votes are the main way generative AI models are compared. Public arenas show visitors two anonymous
answers to the same prompt and rank models by the votes ( Chiang et al., 2024 ; Termignon et al., 2026 ) . The votes are read
as judgments of each model’s text, and where delivery might matter, faster answers are expected to gain. The designers of
compar:IA, the French government’s arena, write that “Faster responses may be perceived as more fluent or reliable, while
slower responses may negatively impact user preference independently of content quality” ( Termignon et al., 2026 ) .
People judge slowly produced algorithmic predictions as less accurate ( Efendić et al., 2020 ) , responsiveness in LLM
applications “is widely assumed to be critical” ( Tan et al., 2026 ) , and decades of research on system response
time link longer delays to lower satisfaction, weaker intentions to return, and less use ( Miller, 1968 ; Shneiderman, 1984 ; Guynes, 1988 ; Palmer, 2002 ; Galletta et al., 2004 ; Nah, 2004 ) .
A second reading treats time as a sign of deliberation and care. People rate products as better when they believe more
effort went into them ( Kruger et al., 2004 ; Morales, 2005 ) , and in a recent laboratory study, participants who
waited 2 seconds for a chatbot’s answer to begin rated its answers as less thoughtful than participants who waited 9 or
20 seconds ( Tan et al., 2026 ) .

blocks.en:
Research on how output is presented gives reasons to expect the opposite of the speed reading for an answer that
appears at once instead of unfolding on screen. Displays of work raise the value people place on a service even when the
results are identical, an effect called the labor illusion ( Buell and Norton, 2011 ) . Users rate a recommendation agent
higher when they perceive that it put more effort into its recommendations ( Tsekouras et al., 2022 ) , and beliefs
about the effort that went into a product help explain why consumers value AI-made products less ( Rix et al., 2025 ) . Research on waiting interfaces offers a second reason: displays that run during a wait hold
attention and immerse users ( Lee et al., 2012 ) , and generative AI responses presented word by word are accepted more
readily than responses presented line by line, because users feel more immersed ( Jin and Gong, 2026 ) . In an experiment
with AI writing tools, Zhou et al. (2025) expected the judged quality of a text not to vary with how it appeared
on screen; they found a small effect instead, with the highest ratings at a pace slightly faster than reading. Whether
such effects reach the blind choices that rank models, and in which direction, is not known.

blocks.en:
Generative AI makes this question a routine operating decision. In the experiments that established the labor
illusion, the display of work was an animation shown while users waited for the result, such as a list of airlines
being searched while a travel site prepared its fares ( Buell and Norton, 2011 ) . In a chatbot, the display is the answer
itself: streaming shows the text as it is written, and it is the default for nearly every answer. Operators can remove
it without changing a word. A response cache returns a stored answer that costs almost nothing to produce, and it can
show that answer at once or at any pace. Platforms already experiment with how generated output is revealed ( Jiang et al., 2026 ) . If delivery moves blind votes, decisions that operators make for cost reasons, such as serving
stored answers, also change how good their answers seem, and with them the preference data used to rank models. This
paper asks how the delivery of the same answer, and the time an answer takes, change the votes that rank AI models and
whether users keep asking.

generate, difficult questions draw long answers, and reasoning models are slow and strong at once. A correlation
between waiting and satisfaction says little about what waiting does. Laboratory studies break that link, but they
assign tasks that participants must complete, so whether participants keep asking reflects the task as much as the
experience.

blocks.en:
This paper uses three sources of variation in natural use that separate how long an answer takes from what it says.
The first is a lottery built into compar:IA, a public chatbot arena run by the French Ministry of Culture, in which
visitors put one prompt to two anonymous models and compare their answers side by side ( Termignon et al., 2026 ) . From March 2026, when a model had already answered the same opening prompt, the
platform drew a random number. Depending on the draw, it either generated a new answer, which the visitor watched
being written, or replayed a stored earlier answer from the same model to the same prompt, which filled the screen in
a fraction of a second.
Replays reproduce earlier fresh answers word for word, and many stored texts appear in the data both as a fresh answer
and as a replay, so the comparison can also be made for the identical text. The second source is congestion. During our
study window the platform’s server waited on each model provider in a way that let a slow provider hold up other
requests, and provider load varied from day to day. Answers of the same length from the same model therefore took
different times to arrive for reasons outside the visitor’s control. The third source is WildChat, a corpus of several
million ChatGPT conversations whose logs record when each reply was created at the provider and when it was received
in full ( Zhao et al., 2024 ) . There, too, provider congestion moves the wait for otherwise similar replies.

blocks.en:
Three findings emerge. First, answers shown at once lost blind votes. Against a fresh answer, a replayed answer
won 22 % of decisive votes, those that picked one answer rather than declaring a tie. Comparing answers
to the same prompt, a replay lowered the chance of winning a decisive vote by 25.8 percentage points
(standard error 4.4), and among all eligible answers it lowered the share that won the conversation and
raised the share that lost it. The penalty persisted when
the same stored text was compared with itself. Averaged over 265 texts, the identical text won
57 % of its decisive votes when it was shown fresh and 29 % when it was replayed,
and voters called it less complete and more often superficial and incorrect when it was replayed. Second, among
answers unfolding on screen, waiting earned no detectable net credit. An answer that took longer than usual for its length
did not win more often, and the estimates rule out gains of more than about 1.4 points for a
doubling of the wait. Third, waiting has a behavioral cost. A slower first exchange lowered the chance that the visitor
asked a second question by 1.8 points per log unit of delay (about 8 % of the base rate), or 1.3 points for each doubling of the wait. Most of the loss came in the slowest fifth of waits. In WildChat, replies slowed by congestion made users less likely
to continue, also when the comparison is limited to models used in the same clock hour.

blocks.en:
These results run against both expectations about blind votes. Delivery moved them, in the direction opposite to the one the arena’s designers anticipated. For the same text, a rapid replay instead of a fresh stream cut the share
of decisive wins roughly in half, and voters explained their choice in the language of substance. The time an answer
took did not move the vote detectably and showed up instead in whether users kept asking. Because a vote compares two
answers, a delay that slows both cannot register in it, although users still pay for it in follow-up questions they do
not ask.

blocks.en:
The paper makes two theoretical contributions and one practical contribution. First, it shows in the field that how an
AI system reveals its output enters consequential judgments of that output with the wording held fixed. Research on the
labor illusion and on presentation has shown such effects on the value placed on a service and on laboratory ratings ( Buell and Norton, 2011 ; Zhou et al., 2025 ; Jin and Gong, 2026 ) . Here they move blind choices between models, by a wide margin, and in
the direction opposite to the reading of speed as fluency or competence ( Efendić et al., 2020 ; Termignon et al., 2026 ) . Second, it bounds what time adds once an answer is being written.
Slowdowns caused by congestion bought no detectable net credit in the vote, so the credit that laboratory evidence finds
for a later first word ( Tan et al., 2026 ) does not extend to them, while they cost follow-up questions. Third, the
results bear on how AI systems are built and evaluated. Caching changes how answers are judged, latency changes whether
users keep asking, and preference leaderboards built from blind votes register how answers are delivered while missing
the cost of waiting.

blocks.en: 2 Theory and Hypotheses
blocks.zh: 2 理论和假设

blocks.en:
How an AI service delivers an answer is a design choice. The operator can stream a fresh answer as the model writes it,
serve stored text at once, or let a slower model take its time. This section places that choice in recent research on
the design of AI agents, sets out the accounts that predict how the delivery of the same answer and the time an answer
takes affect judgments of it, and derives the competing predictions that the three studies test.

blocks.en: 2.1 The delivery of AI answers as a design choice
blocks.zh: 2.1 国家 作为设计选择的AI解答

blocks.en:
Research in information systems and management has shown that the design cues of AI agents change how users evaluate
them and what users do. Human-like cues in a retailer’s customer service chatbot changed whether customers accepted its
offers ( Schanke et al., 2021 ) . Positive emotion expressed by an AI agent did less for service evaluations than
the same emotion from a human employee, in part because it violated what customers expected of an AI agent ( Han et al., 2023 ) . Response time is one such cue. In a laboratory experiment, a delayed chatbot response had opposing
effects on users’ sense of social presence and on their usage intentions, and the effects differed between novice and
experienced users ( Gnewuch et al., 2022 ) . In a field experiment in customer service chats, customers who had just
seen a chatbot fail to understand them read unusually rapid replies from AI-assisted human agents as a sign that they
were still talking to a chatbot, and their sentiment fell ( Zhang and Narayandas, 2026 ) . Between people, fast replies signal
responsiveness and raise the chance of being hired ( Hart et al., 2026 ) .

blocks.en:
Generative AI adds a cue of its own: how the output is revealed. Platforms that generate content in seconds have begun
to experiment with how much of it to show and when, and in one field experiment revealing part of a generated output
before registration raised engagement more than revealing all of it ( Jiang et al., 2026 ) . These studies vary the source of an output, the agent’s social
cues or how much of the output is shown, and the experiments closest to ours vary how the same text appears on screen
( Section 2.3 ). What none observes is the same model’s verbatim answer delivered in two ways under a real
operating policy and judged against another answer in a choice that ranks models.
blocks.zh:
Generative AI增加了自己的提示:输出是如何被揭示的. 以秒计生成内容的平台已经开始
用于实验其中要显示多少以及何时,并在一个现场实验中揭示一部分产生的输出
注册前的约定不仅仅是披露所有约定(Jiang等人,2026年)。 这些研究改变了产出的来源, 代理的社交
提示或显示多少输出, 和我们最接近的实验会改变屏幕上同一文本的显示方式
(第2.3节) 没有人注意到的是,同一个模型的逐字回答是以两种方式在真正的
在对模型进行排序的选择中,操作政策和根据另一个答案进行判断。

blocks.en: 2.2 Speed and time as information about an answer
blocks.zh: 2.2 速度和时间作为答复的信息

blocks.en:
A common account holds that people read the time an answer takes as information about the answer. It comes in two
versions with opposite signs. In the first, speed signals fluency and competence. The designers of compar:IA expect that
“Faster responses may be perceived as more fluent or reliable, while slower responses may negatively impact user
preference independently of content quality” ( Termignon et al., 2026 ) . People judge slowly generated predictions
from algorithms as less accurate and rely on them less. Slowness signals effort for algorithms as for people, but because
prediction is seen as easy for an algorithm, the effort does not count toward quality ( Efendić et al., 2020 ) . Practice
takes the same view: responsiveness in LLM applications “is widely assumed to be critical” ( Tan et al., 2026 ) .
Research on human–computer interaction treated response time as a central design parameter from the start. Miller (1968) proposed thresholds for conversational transactions, and Shneiderman (1984) reviewed evidence that longer and more variable delays slow users down and frustrate them. Delays raise users’ anxiety ( Guynes, 1988 ) , and the search for one acceptable response time has continued for decades ( Dabrowski and Munson, 2011 ) . Information systems research carried the question to the web. Download delay is one of the
performance metrics that predict a web site’s success, including the likelihood that users return ( Palmer, 2002 ) . In controlled experiments, longer page delays reduced users’ performance, attitudes and
behavioral intentions ( Galletta et al., 2004 ) , and users’ tolerance for waiting is short ( Nah, 2004 ) .
Search engines and large web sites report the same pattern: slower result pages change how people interact with them ( Arapakis et al., 2014 ) , and online experiments repeatedly show that speed matters for engagement ( Kohavi et al., 2014 ) .
blocks.zh:
一个常见的说法认为,人们读取一个答案作为答案信息的时间。 分两步走
带有相反标志的版本。 第一,速度信号流畅度和能力。 比较器的设计者:IA期望
“更快的反应可能被认为更流利或可靠,而较慢的反应可能对用户产生不利影响
(Termignon等人,2026年). 人们慢慢地判断产生预测
从算法上看,它不太准确,对它的依赖也较少。 对算法和对人来说 缓慢的信号是努力的 但因为
对于算法来说,预测是容易的,但这种努力并不考虑质量(Efendić等人,2020年)。 实践
采取同样的观点:LLM应用中的响应性“被广泛认为是关键”(Tan等人,2026年)。
关于人机交互的研究从一开始就将响应时间作为中央设计参数. 米勒(1968年)提出了对话交易的阈值,Shneiderman(1984年)审查了关于更长和更多可变的延迟使用户减慢和挫败的证据. 延迟会提高用户的焦虑(Guynes,1988年),寻找一个可接受的响应时间持续了几十年(Dabrowski和Munson,2011年). 信息系统研究将这一问题带入网络。 下载延迟是其中之一
预测网站成功与否的业绩计量,包括用户返回的可能性(Palmer,2002年)。 在有控制的实验中,较长的页面延迟降低了用户的性能、态度和
行为意图(Galletta等人,2004年),用户对等待的容忍度很短(Nah,2004年)。
搜索引擎和大型网站报告的模式相同:结果页较慢改变人们如何与它们互动(Arapakis等人,2014年),在线实验反复显示参与的速度很重要(Kohavi等人,2014年)。

blocks.en:
In the second version, time signals deliberation and care. People rate a poem or a painting more highly when told that
it took longer to make ( Kruger et al., 2004 ) , and observers judge others’ decisions by how much thought went into
them, preferring the amount of thinking that fits the difficulty of the task ( Kupor et al., 2014 ) . For large
language models, Tan et al. (2026) varied the time before the first word of a streamed answer appeared.
Participants who waited 2 seconds rated the answers as less thoughtful than participants who waited 9 or 20 seconds,
and as less useful than those who waited 9 seconds; ratings after 9 and 20 seconds did not differ, and logged
interaction behavior did not change with the delay. The authors conclude that latency is “a tunable design variable”.
blocks.zh:
在第二个版本中,时间提示着考虑和关心. 别人对诗歌或画的评价比较高
(Kruger等人,2004年),观察员们根据对他人的决定的思考程度来判断。
他们更喜欢符合任务难度的思考(Kupor等人,2014年)。 为大
语言模型 Tan et al. (2026) 流化答案的第一个词出现之前的时间变化.
等待2秒的参与者将答案评为比等待9秒或20秒的参与者没有那么深思熟虑,
不如那些等待9秒的人有用;9秒和20秒之后的收视率没有差别,并且记录了
交互行为没有随延迟而改变。 提交人的结论是,耐久性是“可捕性设计变量”。

blocks.en: 2.3 Progressive display
blocks.zh: 2.3 渐进显示

blocks.en:
Modern chatbots stream each answer to the screen as the model produces it, so the user watches the text unfold at the
pace at which the machine writes it. We call this progressive display . In a chatbot it differs from the displays
studied in services in two ways. The display is the answer itself rather than an animation beside it, so what unfolds
on the screen is the substance the user will judge. And it is the default: users see nearly every answer written out,
an answer that appears at once is the exception, and the operator decides when that happens, typically to avoid the cost
of generating the same answer again. Streaming exists to make answers start sooner, not to show the work, so we do not
treat it as operational transparency by design. The contrast our data observe is between a fresh answer streamed as it
was generated and a stored answer replayed in a fraction of a second.
blocks.zh:
现代聊天员在模型生成时对屏幕进行逐个回答,因此用户在屏幕上观看文字的展开
机器写它的速度。 我们称之为进步的展示。 在聊天台上,它与显示不同
以两种方式在服务业学习。 展示是答案本身 而不是旁边的动画, 所以什么展开
屏幕上是用户判断的物质。 而这是默认的: 用户看到几乎所有的答案,
一次出现的答案是例外,操作员决定何时发生,通常是为了避免费用
再次生成相同的答案。 流水是为了让答案更早开始,而不是展示作品,所以我们不
把它作为业务透明度来看待。 我们观测到的数据的对比 是在新答案之间
生成并重放一个存储的答案 。

blocks.en:
Two lines of research predict that an answer which unfolds is judged better than the same answer shown at once. The
first runs through effort. Research on the labor illusion finds that people credit the work they can see ( Buell and Norton, 2011 ) . On simulated travel and dating web sites, users who watched a display of the work being done while
they waited valued the service more than users who received identical results at once. The value came from the display
rather than from the work: varying how many sites the service actually searched did not change how much users valued
it, while showing the search did. The display needed a wait, since there is nothing to show when results arrive at once,
and so the headline finding is that people “can actually prefer websites with longer waits to those that return
instantaneous results” ( Buell and Norton, 2011 ) . Yet time added nothing once the display was present. When the same work
was shown over waits of 10 to 60 seconds, value was higher with the display at every wait and tended to fall as the wait
grew, with no interaction between the two. Consumers reward firms that visibly exert effort for them ( Morales, 2005 ) , and operational transparency can create value for customers and employees alike ( Buell et al., 2017 ) . The logic also reaches machines: users rate a recommendation agent higher when they
perceive that it put more effort into its recommendations ( Tsekouras et al., 2022 ) , and beliefs about the effort
that went into a product help explain why consumers value AI-made products less ( Rix et al., 2025 ) . Customers
also read the speed of a reply as evidence of how it was produced ( Zhang and Narayandas, 2026 ) . On this route, an answer shown at once looks as if
less work went into it, and people judge the quality of work partly by the effort they think it took ( Kruger et al., 2004 ) .
blocks.zh:
有两条研究线预言,一个展开的答案比同时显示的同一答案得到更好的判断. 那个
首先要努力进行。 对劳动幻觉的研究发现,人们会赞扬他们能看到的工作(Buell和Norton,2011年)。 在模拟旅行和约会网址上,观看正在完成的工作的用户
他们等待的服务比一次得到相同结果的用户更加珍视。 值来自显示
而不是来自作品:服务实际搜索多少网站并不改变用户的价值
它,同时显示搜索。 显示需要等待, 因为没有什么可以显示 当结果一到,
所以头条的发现是,人们“实际上可以更喜欢等待时间更长的网站而不是那些返回的网站。
(Buell和Norton,2011年). 然而,当展示出现时,时间却一无所获。 当同一个工作
显示在10至60秒的等待中,值随着每个等待的显示而更高,并随着等待而下降
成长,两人之间没有互动. 消费者奖励明显为其努力的公司(Morales,2005年),业务透明度可以为客户和雇员创造价值(Buell等人,2017年)。 逻辑也到达机器: 用户将推荐代理评分较高
(Tsekouras等人,2022年),以及对这一努力的信念。
(Rix等人,2025年)。 客户
还读了回信的速度,作为如何制作的证据(张和Narayandas,2026). 在这个路线上,一个一次显示的答案看起来像
工作减少,人们根据他们认为付出的努力来判断工作的质量(Kruger等人,2004年)。

blocks.en:
The second route runs through reading and attention. Interfaces that run during a wait hold attention and induce
focused immersion ( Lee et al., 2012 ) , and cues that convey progress reduce uncertainty while animated ones draw
attention away from the wait ( Lee et al., 2017 ) . Generative AI responses presented word by word are accepted more
readily than responses presented line by line, because users feel more immersed, although less so when users need to
understand the content ( Jin and Gong, 2026 ) . In an experiment with AI writing tools that assigned the same texts to
different presentation speeds, Zhou et al. (2025) expected that “There will be no variance between the judged
quality of the text”. They found a small effect instead. The pace rated highest for quality, slightly faster than
average reading speed, was also the one rated most comfortable to read. On this route, text that unfolds at a readable
pace is easier to follow, and a block that appears at once is skimmed or looks like a stock answer.
blocks.zh:
第二条路线贯穿阅读和关注. 等待期间运行的界面保持注意并诱导
重点浸润(Lee等人,2012年),以及传递进展的提示,减少不确定性,同时动画画画
注意远离等待(Lee et al., 2017). 逐字给出的General AI回复被更多接受
与逐行提交的答复相比,用户感觉受浸得更多,尽管在用户需要时情况较少
了解内容(龚和,2026). 在一项AI写作工具的实验中,将同样的文本分配给了
不同的呈现速度, 周等. (2025年)预计“审判结果不会出现差异。
案文的质量”。 他们发现一个小效果代替。 质量评分最高的速度,略高于
平均阅读速度也是被评为最舒适的阅读速度. 在此路径中, 文本在可读状态下展开
速度比较容易跟上,同时出现的区块被省略或看起来像一个股票答案。

blocks.en:
The two routes differ in what the display must do: the first needs it to be taken as a sign of the work behind this
answer, the second only needs the text to be easier to follow. Both predict that the answer shown at once is judged
worse. Our data record votes, the qualifiers voters attach to them, reactions and later actions, so they test whether
progressive display is credited, not which route carries the credit; Section 7.5 describes a test that would
separate them. Both routes also predict that extra time adds nothing once the answer is unfolding: the displayed work is
the same text whether it takes longer or not, and a pace slower than reading makes the text no easier to follow.
blocks.zh:
两种路线在展示必须做什么上有所不同:首先需要把它当作是幕后工作的标志
回答,第二个只需要文本更容易遵循。 两人都预言 立即给出答案
更惨 我们的数据记录了投票情况, 选民对投票的附加条件, 反应和后来的行动,
累进显示记账,而不是记账的路线;第7.5节说明将进行的测试
把他们分开 两条路线还预测,一旦答案出现,额外时间不会增加任何内容:显示的作品是
文本是否需要更长的时间,与阅读速度相比,速度较慢,使得文本不会更容易遵循。

blocks.en: 2.4 Competing predictions
blocks.zh: 2.4 相互竞争的预测

blocks.en:
Table 1 sets out what the accounts predict. The first observable is how the same answer fares when it is
shown at once rather than unfolding. If votes judge only the text, as Zhou et al. (2025) expected for ratings,
the two should do equally well. If speed signals fluency or competence, as compar:IA’s designers expected, the answer
shown at once should do at least as well. If progressive display is credited, it should do worse.
blocks.zh:
表1列出了账目的预测。 第一个观察点是 当答案是相同的时
显示在瞬间,而不是出现。 如果投票只判断文本,如周等人. (2025年)收视率
两者应该做同样好。 如果速度显示流畅度或能力,作为比较: IA的设计者预期,答案
一次显示至少也应该如此。 如果渐进显示被记为功劳,它应该做得更糟.

blocks.en:
H1a (progressive display). An AI answer shown at once is judged worse than a comparable answer that unfolds on
screen as it is generated. H1b (text only, or speed as fluency). An AI answer shown at once is judged no worse than a comparable answer
that unfolds on screen as it is generated.
blocks.zh:
H1a(渐进显示). 一次显示的AI答案比一次显示的可比答案更糟糕
屏幕正在生成。 H1b(仅文本,或速度为流利). 立即显示的AI答案 被评为不比可比答案差
它在屏幕上展开 当它产生。

blocks.en:
The qualifiers that voters can attach to a vote, such as complete, superficial or incorrect, show how they explain their
choice. We use them to describe the judgment, not to tell the routes apart.
blocks.zh:
选民可以附加在选票上的限定词,如完整、肤浅或不正确,表明他们如何解释他们的投票。
选择。 我们用它们来描述判断,而不是分辨路线.

blocks.en:
The second observable is the time taken by answers that unfold on screen. Here the two readings of time part ways, and
progressive display predicts no change.
blocks.zh:
第二个可观测到的是屏幕上的答案所花费的时间。 在这里,两读 时间部分方式,和
渐进显示预示不变。

blocks.en: H2a (time as deliberation). Among answers that unfold on screen, an answer that takes longer is judged better. H2b (time as a cost). Among answers that unfold on screen, an answer that takes longer is judged worse.
blocks.zh: H2a(作为审议时间). 在屏幕上流传的答案中,一个需要更长时间的答案被判断得更好. H2b(时间作为成本). 在屏幕上流传的答案中,一个需要更长时间的答案被判断得更糟.

blocks.en:
A result between the two would fit progressive display. It would also arise if a credit for deliberation and a cost of waiting cancelled, so the second observable bounds the net effect of time on the vote rather than identifying
its parts.
blocks.zh:
两者的结果将适合渐进显示。 如果一笔审议费和等待费被取消,也会出现这种情况,因此第二个可观察到的对表决时间的净影响,而不是确定
它的部件。

blocks.en:
The third observable is behavior. A chatbot conversation is a sequence of service encounters: after each answer the
user decides whether to start another one. Research on queues finds that delays lower customers’ evaluations of a
service, largely through anger and uncertainty ( Taylor, 1994 ) , and that longer waits lead people to abandon
service, whether patients in an emergency department ( Batt and Terwiesch, 2015 ) or callers to a call center ( Akşin et al., 2013 ) . If time is a cost, a costly wait for one answer makes the next encounter less attractive.
blocks.zh:
第三个观察是行为。 聊天人对话是服务遭遇的顺序:每次回答后
用户决定是否再启动一个。 对队列的研究发现,延迟了客户对
服务,主要是通过愤怒和不确定(Taylor,1994年),而等待更长的时间导致人们放弃
服务,无论是急诊部的病人(Batt和Terwisch,2015年)还是呼叫中心(Akşin等人,2013年)。 如果时间是一种代价,那么等待一个答案的代价高昂,那么下一次遭遇就不那么有吸引力。

blocks.en: H3 (cost of time). A longer wait for an AI answer lowers the chance that the user continues the conversation.
blocks.zh: H3(时间成本). 长时间等待AI的回答会降低用户继续对话的机会.

blocks.en:
H3 does not tell the accounts of H1 apart. It locates where the cost of time appears, and it matters for evaluation:
a vote compares two answers, so a delay that slows both cannot change which one wins, while the decision to ask again
registers it.
blocks.zh:
H3没有将H1的账户分开。 它位于时间成本出现的地方,评价很重要:
一个投票比较两个答案,所以延迟 既慢又慢 无法改变谁赢了, 而决定再次问
登记它。

blocks.en: 2.5 Preferences as the yardstick for AI systems
blocks.zh: 2.5 以优惠作为AI系统的尺度

blocks.en:
These questions also bear on how generative AI is evaluated. Public arenas show visitors two anonymous answers to the
same prompt and aggregate their votes into leaderboards ( Chiang et al., 2024 ; Termignon et al., 2026 ) . Human
preferences of this kind respond to features other than accuracy, most prominently answer length ( Singhal et al., 2024 ) , and, as noted above, the designers of compar:IA expect latency to influence judgments too ( Termignon et al., 2026 ) . Whether such influences are a problem depends on what a leaderboard is meant to
measure. If it measures the quality of the text a model writes, how the text is delivered is a confound. If it
measures the service a user experiences, delivery belongs in the score, but then the cost of a slow model should
appear in it, and a vote cast after the wait may not register the follow-up questions the wait has cost.
blocks.zh:
这些问题还关系到如何评价基因AI。 公共竞技场显示 访客的两个匿名回答
他们的选票同样迅速并汇总到领导板上(Chiang et al., 2024;Termignon et al., 2026). 人类
这类偏好对准确性以外的特征作出反应,最突出的回答长度(Singhal等人,2024年),如上文所述,比较器的设计者: 国际律师协会预计,延迟也会影响判决(Termignon等人,2026年)。 这种影响是否是一个问题取决于领导板的意图是什么
计量。 如果它衡量一个模型所写的文本的质量,那么如何交付文本就是一个困惑。 如果是这样
衡量用户体验的服务,交付属于分数,但慢模式的成本应该
在等待之后进行的投票可能无法登记等待费用的后续问题。

blocks.en: 3 Setting and Data
blocks.zh: 3 设置和数据

blocks.en: 3.1 compar:IA
blocks.zh: 3.1 比较:IA

blocks.en:
compar:IA is a public service developed inside the French government to let the general public compare
conversational AI models and to collect French-language preference data ( Termignon et al., 2026 ) . No account is
needed, and the platform is widely used in schools and universities. A visitor types a prompt, or picks a suggested
one, and chooses how the two models are drawn: at random, from a list the visitor selects, or within themes such as
large versus small models or reasoning models. Two anonymous models then answer side by side. The two answers appear together once both models have begun to
answer. Each is then shown on screen as its text arrives, with a loading indicator until the model finishes, and for
reasoning models the reasoning text appears in a panel above the answer. 1 1 1 We read the interface and the
server’s behavior from the platform’s public source code and its commit history ( compar:IA team, 2026 ) . Appendix B lists the code changes that matter for our designs, with links to them and their merge
dates. The visitor can then ask a follow-up question, which goes to both
models, or react to any individual answer with a thumbs-up or thumbs-down and optional qualifiers (useful, complete,
creative, clear formatting; incorrect, superficial, instructions not followed). If no message reaction was given, the
visitor can also cast a final vote for one model or declare the two equal, again with optional qualifiers. The models’ identities are
revealed only after this feedback.

Two features of how the platform ran during our window matter for the design, and both are documented in its

blocks.en:
From March 2026 the platform kept a cache, a store of earlier first answers, to reduce its costs ( compar:IA team, 2026 ) . The store
was keyed by the model and the text of the opening prompt, with surrounding spaces removed and capital letters
ignored; it held up to the five most recent answers for each key and expired 48 hours after the key was last used.
For each of the two answers in a conversation, the platform drew a random number. With a fixed probability it looked
for the key in the store and, if the key was there, replayed one of the stored answers, chosen at random; otherwise it
asked the model for a fresh answer, which was then added to the store. The first replay in the data occurs on
16 March 2026, and our window runs to 18 May 2026. Appendix B documents the code that ran in this window.

blocks.en:
A fresh answer was written on screen at the pace at which the model produced it. A replay was meant to look similar:
the code breaks the stored text into about fifteen pieces and “yields with small delays to mimic real streaming
behavior for consistent UX” ( compar:IA team, 2026 ) . In practice the delays were cut short. The server read the two
answers of a comparison together and, as the developers later explained, “the slower read was cancelled as soon as
the other model answered,” which ended the replay’s pause each time the other answer produced text. The recorded
durations, which the server measured from the start of the replay to its last piece, show the result
( Fig. 1 ). The median replay took 0.3 seconds, and three quarters took at most
1.1 seconds. The median fresh answer to the same set of prompts took 4.3 seconds
(interquartile range 1.4 to 20.3 seconds). Within the same model and prompt, a
replay shortened the recorded duration by 1.7 log units, a factor of more than five. A replayed
answer therefore filled its side of the screen in a fraction of a second, far faster than a reader can follow text
being written, while the answer beside it was usually still being written. For reasoning models, the stored reasoning
text appeared in one piece. We call this treatment a replay and compare it with fresh generation.

A replay reproduces an answer that the same model gave earlier to the same prompt, and
that earlier answer was itself shown fresh to another visitor. The data therefore contain repeated appearances of the
same stored text, some written on screen and some replayed. 1,948 stored texts appear in both forms, and
265 of them received decisive votes in both forms: 310 fresh and
334 replayed appearances, judged by 445 visitors across 118 prompts. The texts match in the answer itself, including its formatting. For the 28 % of texts that
came with reasoning, the reasoning had the same length in every appearance in 88 % of cases. A
replay came a median of 0.9 hours after the fresh appearance of its text. Weighting each text
equally, the same text won 57 % of its decisive votes when it was shown fresh and
29 % when it was replayed, a difference of 27.3 points (3.7). With fixed
effects for the text, a replay lowered its chance of winning by 29.8 points (2.8; Table 4 c). The estimate is similar with standard errors clustered by text (3.5) and with fixed
effects for the opponent’s model and a control for the length of its answer (30.2 points). It is
also similar when replays are limited to the first 48 hours after the fresh appearance (28.0 points) and among the 44 texts whose fresh and replayed appearances were all eligible for the
draw (28.2 points; 9.1 clustered by text). The identical text also drew
fewer thumbs-up and more thumbs-down when it was replayed. This comparison holds the words fixed rather
than drawing the delivery at random, so it complements the lottery: it shows that differences between texts do not
account for the penalty.

Generation time depends on the model, on how long the answer is and on how much the model reasons before answering.
We measure slowness as the part of an answer’s log generation time that these do not explain: the residual from
a regression of log duration on log answer length and log reasoning length, estimated separately for each model in
each month. An answer with slowness 0 took as long as is typical for that model and that much text; slowness of 0.7
means it took about twice as long. The standard deviation of slowness is 0.65 log units.

blocks.en:
Slowness can still reflect content, for example if some kinds of text are slower to produce. We therefore use a
measure of congestion as an instrument: the average slowness of the same model’s answers to other visitors on the same
day, leaving out the focal visitor’s own answers. Because the platform’s server and each model provider were shared
by all visitors, a busy day for a provider slowed every answer from that model ( Section 3 ). The regressions
absorb a fixed effect for each calendar day, so the identifying variation is the difference between a model’s
congestion and that of other models on the same day; it has a standard deviation of 0.10 log units after
the fixed effects. Congestion is measured net of answer length because raw generation times also carry the day’s mix
of requests: a congestion measure built from raw times predicts longer answers from the focal models
(+0.034 log units per log unit, standard error 0.017), whereas the length-adjusted measure does not
( Table 12 ). We report ordinary least squares (OLS) estimates, which use all variation in slowness, and
instrumental-variable (IV) estimates, which use only the variation driven by congestion. The IV estimates rest on two
assumptions. The first is that, given the
fixed effects, a model’s congestion on a given day is unrelated to who visited and what they asked. The second is that
congestion affects what visitors do only through the time the answer takes.

describe different timing changes and do not lie on one estimated curve.

blocks.en: 6.1 Design
blocks.zh: 6.1 设计

blocks.en:
For each reply we compute the latency as the time WildChat’s server received the full reply minus the time the
provider created the completion, both recorded to the second ( Section 3 ). Of the 5,167,182 replies in the
release, none has a negative latency, 461,750 have a latency below one second, recorded as zero, and only
26 exceed ten minutes. Latency tracks reply length closely: within model and month, one log
unit of additional reply length goes with 0.61 log units of additional latency, as expected if latency
covers the writing of the complete reply. We keep replies with latencies of up to ten minutes and remove hashed IP
addresses that created more than 50 conversations on a single day. The sample contains 4,378,514 replies in
2,694,924 conversations from 1,829,326 hashed IP addresses, from April 2023 to July 2025. The median
reply took 6 seconds (interquartile range 2 to 13 seconds; 95th
percentile 43 seconds). The outcome is whether the user sent another message in the same
conversation after the reply. Users did so after 17.6 % of first replies and after
73.5 % of later replies.

blocks.en:
The design mirrors Study 2 with one change. Short replies carry a fixed overhead and many latencies are recorded as
zero, so we measure slowness on the log of one plus the latency in seconds and adjust for content non-parametrically.
Slowness is that log minus its average among replies from the same model in the same month with similar reply
length, similar message length and the same position in the conversation. Congestion is the average slowness of the
same model’s replies to other users in the same clock hour. OpenAI’s service was shared by all WildChat users and by
the provider’s other customers, so hourly congestion varies for reasons outside any one user’s control.

Congestion also tracks demand: with calendar-day and hour-of-week effects, congested hours carried shorter messages
and replies and fewer users in the United States ( Table 12 ). The preferred specification therefore absorbs a

the comparison is between models used in the same hour; demand specific to one model remains. The
59 % of replies sent in hours when more than one model was in use provide the identifying
variation. blocks.en: 7 Discussion
blocks.zh: 7 讨论情况

blocks.en:
The three studies separate two things that usually travel together: how an AI answer is delivered and how long the
user waits for it. Delivery moved the vote. Weighting each text equally, the same stored text from the same model won
57 % of its decisive votes when it unfolded on screen and 29 % when it filled the
screen at once. Voters explained their choices against the replayed text by calling it less complete, more superficial
and more often incorrect. Waiting moved behavior. Among answers that unfolded on screen, extra waiting
brought no detectable net credit in the vote, and long waits made people less likely to keep asking, both on a public
arena and in everyday ChatGPT use.

blocks.en:
Table 10 sets each account against the results that bear on it. Votes that judge only the text, and votes
that favor faster answers, both fail the first test: the answer shown at once lost, by a wide margin, and voters did not
describe it as the more reliable one. Progressive display passes it. On the time an unfolding answer takes, neither
reading of time finds detectable support in the vote, which is what progressive display predicts. The cost of time appears instead in whether users
asked again.

blocks.en:
Several features of the setting could produce a penalty for answers shown at once without any of these accounts, and
the data rule them out. The penalty appears on single answers when both answers in a conversation were replays, so it
does not require a visibly working answer on the other side of the screen, although the contrast with such an answer
made it larger. Among answers that unfolded, the one that finished later did not win more often, so the penalty is not a
recency effect. The identical text drew it, and it survived the exclusion of prompts that depend on the date, so stored
content does not explain it. Replays did not change whether visitors voted or, across all conversations, how often they
declared a tie. Among those who voted, a single replay made a tie less likely, which sharpens the comparison rather than
selecting who votes.

blocks.en: 7.2 Implications for theory
blocks.zh: 7.2 对理论的影响

blocks.en:
The labor illusion holds that people value a service more when they can see the work behind it, and its experiments
showed that the display, not the amount of actual work, carried the effect ( Buell and Norton, 2011 ) . Later work found
that how AI text appears on screen changes laboratory ratings of its quality, by a small margin ( Zhou et al., 2025 ) , and changes users’ willingness to accept it ( Jin and Gong, 2026 ) . Our results carry these
findings into the setting where judgments of AI output have consequences: blind choices that rank models, made by
people who chose their own questions, about the same model’s verbatim answer delivered under an operator’s real
policy. There, delivery moved the outcome by a wide margin, and in the direction opposite to the one the platform’s
designers expected ( Termignon et al., 2026 ) . Research on the discount that consumers apply to AI-made products
traces it in part to beliefs about the love and effort that went into a product an algorithm created ( Rix et al., 2025 ) . Here both answers came from AI and the wording was fixed, so delivery alone moved the outcome. Revealing part of a generated output before
registration raises engagement ( Jiang et al., 2026 ) ; our results add that how the whole answer is revealed changes
how it is judged. The prediction that machines are judged more reliable when fast ( Efendić et al., 2020 ) did not carry over to text that users could see unfold: the answer shown at once was the one
voters described as incorrect more often. For generative AI, whose answers unfold by default, the practical question the
labor illusion raises is reversed: not whether to add a display of work, but when back-end decisions such as caching
take it away. Which route carries the effect is the theoretical question the field data leave open. The answer decides whether the effect reflects an inference about effort, which telling users that the pace is set by software
should weaken, or an easier reading, which it should not.

The results also bound the reading of time as information about machine output. Among answers that unfolded on
screen, slowdowns caused by congestion bought no detectable net credit in the vote. Laboratory evidence that a later
first word raises perceived thoughtfulness ( Tan et al., 2026 ) sits alongside this result rather than against it.
The designs vary different parts of the wait: the laboratory study delayed the first word and held the pace of writing
fixed, the replays in our data removed the unfolding altogether, and congestion lengthened the whole time to the last
word. How a delay before the first word combines with the unfolding of the text remains open, and a design that varies
the two separately would show it. The labor illusion’s own experiments point the same way as our estimate: with the same
work displayed, longer waits added no value ( Buell and Norton, 2011 ) .

blocks.en: 7.3 Implications for design
blocks.zh: 7.3 对设计的影响

blocks.en:
Caching is attractive to every operator of a generative AI service because it saves computation and time ( Bang, 2023 ) . Our results show that how a stored answer is shown matters for how it is judged. An answer
that fills the screen at once is judged worse than the same answer unfolding on screen, so a cache that saves cost can lower
perceived quality. compar:IA’s own design intended to replay stored answers in pieces “to mimic real streaming
behavior” ( compar:IA team, 2026 ) ; the replays in our window ran far faster than intended. The results support
testing replay at a readable pace, and they raise the same question for speculative decoding and other methods that
change the pace at which text appears ( Leviathan et al., 2023 ) . Designed experiments can then identify the pace that serves users best and show
whether a slower display of a stored answer helps users or only raises their opinion of it.

blocks.en: 7.4 Implications for evaluation
blocks.zh: 7.4 对评价的影响

blocks.en:
Preference leaderboards built from blind votes have become a standard yardstick for generative AI ( Chiang et al., 2024 ; Termignon et al., 2026 ) . What delivery means for them depends on what they are meant to measure.
If a leaderboard measures the quality of the text a model writes, delivery is a confound: a model whose answers
happened to be replayed more often would have lost ground for reasons unrelated to its output. Arenas can remove it by
showing every answer under the same display conditions, or record caching, streaming pace and the display of
reasoning and adjust for them, as they already do for answer length ( Singhal et al., 2024 ) . If a leaderboard measures
the service a user experiences, delivery belongs in the score, but then the cost of latency that we measure is missing from it.
The vote showed no detectable reward for slower answers, yet slower answers lowered the chance that the user kept the
conversation going. A preference score cannot register this cost when both answers are slow, because a vote compares
the two: a delay that slows both leaves the winner unchanged, while the user still pays it. Continuation measures such as follow-up rates
belong next to preference scores when systems are compared.

blocks.en: 7.5 Limitations and future work
blocks.zh: 7.5 限制和今后的工作

blocks.en:
Several features of the setting point to directions for future work. First, a replay changes how fast an answer
appears, how it unfolds and how much time the reader has to follow it, all at once, so the field data identify the
effect of this delivery but not the psychological route behind it. The labor illusion proposes inferred effort, while
unfolding text may also help readers follow an answer, hold attention, or make an answer seem written for the request.
A designed experiment could separate these routes: show the same answer on the same schedule, unfolding at a readable
pace or appearing mostly in a final burst, and tell half the readers that software sets the pace independently of the
work the model did. An effect that weakens under this disclosure, while reading comfort holds, points to inferred
effort; one that survives it points to reading. Asking readers how likely a specific, checkable claim is to be correct,
before any overall judgment and with answers of known accuracy, would show whether delivery changes beliefs about
accuracy or only the reasons voters give, which the optional qualifiers in our data cannot settle. Varying the delay
before the first word separately would connect these results to laboratory evidence on onset delay. Second, eligibility for a replay is reconstructed from a public release that omits some conversations, the release
contains only completed answers, and durations are measured on the platform’s server rather than in the visitor’s browser. Logs of every request and of what each visitor saw would sharpen all three. Third, the congestion estimates rest on the assumption that a provider’s load affects visitors only
through the time their answers take. A blocked server can also slow the interface itself, and congestion slightly
shortened reasoning text. In WildChat, a fixed effect for each clock hour absorbs demand shared by all models in that
hour but not demand specific to one model. Providers’ own records of outages and load would offer cleaner variation. Fourth,
continuation is an action, not a measure of satisfaction or benefit: a user may stop because a question was answered.
Linking continuation to task success would show what the lost questions were worth. Fifth, WildChat identifies users
only by hashed IP addresses, and its public release omits conversations that contain toxic content anywhere, which
may relate to how long they ran. Finally, the replay lottery covers prompts that were asked repeatedly, which are
shorter and more often suggested or assigned than the average prompt. compar:IA’s audience is largely French-speaking
and includes many students, and WildChat users chose a free service. Replications with unique, demanding questions,
in commercial assistants and in other languages would show how far the results extend.

blocks.en: 8 Conclusion
blocks.zh: 8 结论

blocks.en:
Is an AI answer worth the wait? In these settings, users gave no detectable net credit in their votes for extra waiting
on answers they watched being written, and long waits made them less likely to keep asking. They did, however, judge answers that
appeared at once more harshly than the same answers unfolding on screen. What moved their votes was how an answer was
delivered, not how long it took. For those who build and evaluate AI systems,
two tests follow: whether showing stored answers at a readable pace removes the penalty, and whether shorter waits keep
users asking. Preference votes register the first and miss the second.

Appendix C Reconstructing Replay Eligibility

blocks.en:
We reconstruct, for every first answer from the first recorded replay onward, whether the store held answers for its
key. An answer is eligible if two conditions hold. First, the same model gave at least one fresh first answer to the same
opening prompt after caching began and before this answer, with prompts compared as the platform compared them, after
removing surrounding spaces and ignoring capital letters. Second, the previous first answer for that model and prompt,
fresh or replayed, came no more than 48 hours earlier. Two sources of error remain. Conversations that are not in the public release, for
example because they were removed for containing personal data ( Termignon et al., 2026 ) , may have created or
refreshed a key that we do not observe. Some answers we classify as ineligible were therefore eligible:
509 of the 8,604 replays in the window (6 %) fall in this group
and are not used. Conversely, a key may have expired early or failed to be written, so that some answers we classify
as eligible could not have been replayed; these are always fresh, and comparing answers to the same prompt limits the
damage they can do. Restricting the vote sample to answers whose key had been used within the previous 24 hours, or to
answers whose store had served a replay within the previous 48 hours, leaves the estimate about the same
( Table 6 ). Matching prompts by their exact text rather than by the platform’s rule identifies
12,057 rather than 12,518 eligible answers across all traffic. Of the 2,460 model–prompt cells in our sample, 474 contain both replayed and fresh answers; they hold
9,339 of the 11,699 eligible answers and provide the comparisons within prompt.
